summary: First checkpoint (GZ.0): the normalisation table for heights, regulators, periods, centres and CM constants, pinned to the Tau Ceti library as it is at f790474. Tau Ceti's canonicalHeight is the (O)-normalised height (½·lim h(x(2ⁿP))/4ⁿ), and its regulator uses the halved pairing, so the BSD regulator (the LMFDB/Müller–Stoll convention) is 2^r times Tau Ceti's regulator (37.a1: 0.0511 against 0.0256). The x-height ĥ_x, the BSD pairing and the BSD regulator are defined, a request goes to EllipticCurves Layer 7, and the discrepancy with Layer 6's pinned normalisation is recorded. Also: Gram-determinant rescaling, the canonical height on E(K) ⊗ ℚ with the trace/average factor, the centres s = 1 and 1/2 and Λ′(E,1), the unit index u = #μ(K)/2, the Artin-map convention, and the full real period with c∞. New source issue GrossZagierAndArithmeticHeights/E1 (Conrad's u_x). GZ.1–GZ.7 are not read.

nodes.title: Rescaling a pairing rescales its Gram determinant by c^r
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring, M an R-module, B : M →ₗ M →ₗ R a bilinear map and v : Fin r → M. For c ∈ R the Gram matrix of c • B on v is c • (Gram matrix of B on v), so det Gram(c • B, v) = c^r · det Gram(B, v). For a real-valued pairing on a free ℤ-module of rank r, the regulator |det Gram| rescales by |c|^r.
hypotheses: R commutative; r the length of the family.
proofSteps: Gram(c • B, v)_{ij} = c·B(v_i, v_j), so the Gram matrix is c • Gram(B, v).
Matrix.det_smul: det(c • A) = c^r det A for an r × r matrix.
Taking absolute values gives the regulator statement.
acceptance: c = 2, r = 1: a rank-one regulator doubles, which is the factor between Tau Ceti's regulator and the BSD regulator (GZ.0/bsd-regulator).
c = [K:ℚ]: passing from absolute heights to heights over K multiplies a rank-r regulator by [K:ℚ]^r.

nodes.title: The x-height canonical height ĥ_x
nodes.statement: For an elliptic curve given by a Weierstrass equation W over a field K with admissible absolute values, the x-height canonical height is ĥ_x(P) = lim_{n→∞} h(x(2ⁿP))/4ⁿ, where h is Tau Ceti's naïve height of the x-coordinate (Point.naiveHeight). It equals 2 · Point.canonicalHeight P, where Tau Ceti's canonicalHeight carries the factor 1/2 and is the height attached to the divisor (O) (Silverman's normalisation). ĥ_x is the height attached to 2(O), and it is the normalisation of Cremona–Prickett–Siksek, Müller–Stoll and the LMFDB, in which the BSD regulator is computed.
proofSteps: Tau Ceti's Point.tendsto_naiveHeight_two_pow_nsmul_div_four_pow: h(2ⁿP)/(2·4ⁿ) tends to canonicalHeight P, so h(2ⁿP)/4ⁿ tends to 2·canonicalHeight P. Hence ĥ_x is a limit, not a junk limUnder value.
Consequences: ĥ_x(nP) = n²ĥ_x(P) (Point.canonicalHeight_nsmul), ĥ_x ≥ 0, and ĥ_x(P) = 0 iff P is torsion.
acceptance: For 37.a1 (y² + y = x³ − x) and P = (0, 0): ĥ_x(P) = 0.0511114082… (LMFDB), so canonicalHeight P = 0.0255557041….

nodes.title: The BSD height pairing
nodes.statement: The BSD height pairing is ⟨P, Q⟩_BSD = ĥ(P + Q) − ĥ(P) − ĥ(Q) with ĥ = Tau Ceti's canonicalHeight, the polar form of the (O)-normalised height. Equivalently it is the halved polar form of ĥ_x, and ⟨P, Q⟩_BSD = 2 · neronTatePairing W P Q, where Tau Ceti's neronTatePairing is QuadraticMap.associated', the halved polar form of ĥ. On the diagonal ⟨P, P⟩_BSD = ĥ_x(P) = 2ĥ(P). This is the pairing whose Gram determinant is the regulator in the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer formula.
proofSteps: ⟨,⟩_BSD = QuadraticMap.polar of canonicalHeightQuadratic, which is bilinear because ĥ satisfies the parallelogram law exactly.
neronTatePairing_apply gives neronTatePairing W P Q = (ĥ(P + Q) − ĥ(P) − ĥ(Q))/2, so ⟨,⟩_BSD = 2 • neronTatePairing W.
On the diagonal: polar(ĥ)(P, P) = ĥ(2P) − 2ĥ(P) = 2ĥ(P) = ĥ_x(P).
acceptance: For 37.a1: ⟨(0,0), (0,0)⟩_BSD = 0.0511114082…, the LMFDB regulator, while neronTatePairing W (0,0) (0,0) = 0.0255557041….

nodes.title: The BSD regulator, and Tau Ceti's regulator
nodes.statement: For W elliptic with E(K)/tors finitely generated of rank r, the BSD regulator is Reg_BSD = |det Gram(⟨,⟩_BSD)| on any ℤ-basis of E(K)/tors, and it equals 2^r · regulator W, where Tau Ceti's regulator is the Gram determinant of the halved pairing neronTatePairing. The Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer quotient is stated with Reg_BSD. Tau Ceti's regulator agrees with it only in rank 0.
hypotheses: W elliptic; [Module.Finite ℤ (PointModTorsion W)]; r = finrank ℤ (PointModTorsion W).
proofSteps: ⟨,⟩_BSD = 2 • neronTatePairing (GZ.0/bsd-height-pairing), so on any basis Gram(⟨,⟩_BSD) = 2 • neronTateGramMatrix.
GZ.0/gram-determinant-rescaling gives |det| = 2^r |det neronTateGramMatrix| = 2^r regulator W (regulator_eq_abs_det_neronTateGramMatrix); basis independence is inherited.
acceptance: 37.a1 (rank 1): Reg_BSD = 0.0511114082… and Ω = 5.9869172924…, so Ω·Reg_BSD = 0.3059997738… = L′(E, 1), with Ш, c_p and torsion all 1 (LMFDB). Tau Ceti's regulator is 0.0255557041… there, and Ω·regulator = L′(E,1)/2.

nodes.title: The dictionary of height conventions
nodes.statement: At the pinned Tau Ceti (f790474): canonicalHeight = ½·lim h_x(2ⁿP)/4ⁿ is the (O)-normalised height (Silverman's); neronTatePairing = QuadraticMap.associated' of it, with ⟨P, P⟩ = canonicalHeight P; regulator = |det| of that Gram matrix. In the normalisation of Cremona–Prickett–Siksek, Müller–Stoll and the LMFDB, ĥ = lim h(x(nP))/n² = 2·canonicalHeight, and the BSD regulator is the Gram determinant of the pairing with ⟨P, P⟩ = that ĥ, so Reg_BSD = 2^r·regulator. Two statements in the Tau Ceti corpus disagree with the implementation. (i) The EllipticCurves roadmap pins 'ĥ(P) = lim_n h(x(n • P))/n²' and says the regulator and BSD quotient are stated against it; the implemented ĥ is half of that. (ii) The CanonicalHeight module says the (O)-height is 'the one the Néron–Tate pairing, the regulator and the BSD formula are stated with'. The BSD formula needs Reg_BSD, which is 2^r times the regulator built from that height's halved pairing. Heights over K versus absolute heights differ by [K:ℚ]; Tau Ceti's naïve height is the Mathlib height of the supplied AdmissibleAbsValues instance, and no number-field instance exists at the pin, so that factor is not yet fixed.
proofSteps: The Tau Ceti side is read off the definitions of canonicalHeight, neronTatePairing and regulator (GZ.0/x-height-canonical-height, GZ.0/bsd-height-pairing, GZ.0/bsd-regulator).
The other side is Müller–Stoll's §3 and Remark 3.1 together with the LMFDB values for 37.a1, where Ω·ĥ_x((0,0)) = L′(E,1) to 30 digits.
acceptance: No consumer infers a factor of 2 from the name 'Néron–Tate': every formula states which of canonicalHeight, xCanonicalHeight, neronTatePairing or bsdHeightPairing it uses.
A BSD consumer that uses Tau Ceti's regulator W directly is off by 2^r; in rank 1 this is a factor of 2 in the 2-part of Ш.

nodes.title: The canonical height on E(K) ⊗ ℚ
nodes.statement: The canonical height extends uniquely to a quadratic form ĥ_ℚ on the ℚ-vector space E(K) ⊗_ℤ ℚ with ĥ_ℚ(P ⊗ q) = q²·ĥ(P); torsion goes to zero. The same holds for ĥ_x and the two pairings. Averages of points, such as a normalised average of a Galois orbit, live here.
proofSteps: ĥ is a ℤ-quadratic map W.Point → ℝ (canonicalHeightQuadratic) and ℝ is a ℚ-vector space; a ℤ-quadratic map into a ℚ-vector space extends uniquely along M → M ⊗ ℚ, because M ⊗ ℚ is the localisation of M at the nonzero integers and ĥ(nP) = n²ĥ(P) forces the value on P ⊗ (1/n).
Torsion maps to zero in M ⊗ ℚ, consistently with ĥ vanishing on torsion.

nodes.title: Trace versus normalised average of a Galois orbit
nodes.statement: Let H/K be a finite Galois extension of degree h and P ∈ E(H). The trace Tr(P) = Σ_{σ ∈ Gal(H/K)} σP lies in E(K), and the normalised average Av(P) = (1/h)·Tr(P) lies in E(K) ⊗ ℚ. Then ĥ_ℚ(Av(P)) = ĥ(Tr P)/h², and the same factor relates any pairing of averages to the pairing of traces. A formula written with averages and one written with traces differ by h² in every height.
hypotheses: H/K Galois of degree h; the heights over H and over K are compared by the same normalisation.
proofSteps: Av(P) = Tr(P) ⊗ (1/h), and GZ.0/canonical-height-rational gives the factor (1/h)².
acceptance: Cai–Shu–Tian take the trace P_K(f) = Tr_{H_K/K} f(P) ∈ E(K); an average-based statement of the same formula carries h_K² in its constant.

sources.excerpt: write PK(f) := TrHK/K f(P) ∈ E(K)
sources.match: The Heegner point over K is a trace, not an average.

nodes.title: The motivic centre s = 1 and the unitary centre s = 1/2
nodes.statement: Let L(E, s) be the motivic L-function of an elliptic curve over ℚ of conductor N (centre s = 1), L(s, π_E) := L(E, s + 1/2) its unitary normalisation (centre s = 1/2), and Λ(E, s) := N^{s/2}·Γ_ℂ(s)·L(E, s) the completed function with Mathlib's Γ_ℂ(s) = 2(2π)^{−s}Γ(s). If L(E, ·) is differentiable at 1 and L(E, 1) = 0, then (d/ds)L(s, π_E) at s = 1/2 equals L′(E, 1), and Λ′(E, 1) = N^{1/2}·π^{−1}·L′(E, 1). With the other common convention Λ = N^{s/2}(2π)^{−s}Γ(s)L, the factor is N^{1/2}(2π)^{−1}.
hypotheses: L(E, ·) differentiable at 1 with L(E, 1) = 0 (the case of odd analytic rank).
proofSteps: The shift s ↦ s + 1/2 has derivative 1.
Product rule (deriv_mul) at a zero of L: (G·L)′(1) = G(1)·L′(1) + G′(1)·L(1) = G(1)·L′(1).
G(1) = N^{1/2}·Γ_ℂ(1) = N^{1/2}·2(2π)^{−1}Γ(1) = N^{1/2}/π (Complex.Gammaℂ_def, Complex.Gamma_one).
acceptance: The factor 2 between Γ_ℂ and (2π)^{−s}Γ(s) is a convention and must be written, not absorbed.
Cai–Shu–Tian write L_v(s, A, M) = L(s − 1/2, π_v) at finite places, and the complete L(s, π_A) includes the archimedean factors.

sources.excerpt: then Lv(s, A, M) = L(s − 1/2, πv) for all finite places v of F
sources.match: The motivic L-function is the automorphic one shifted by 1/2: centre s = 1 against s = 1/2.

nodes.title: The unit index u
nodes.statement: For an imaginary quadratic field K, u(K) = [O_K^× : ℤ^×] = #μ(K)/2, the number that appears squared in the Gross–Zagier constant. In Mathlib terms, u(K) = NumberField.Units.torsionOrder K / 2. So u(K) = 1 except u(ℚ(√−1)) = 2 and u(ℚ(√−3)) = 3.
proofSteps: O_K^× is finite for K imaginary quadratic, so it equals its torsion μ(K), and ℤ^× = {±1} has index #μ(K)/2.
acceptance: Conrad's §1 defines u_x as #μ(K) itself, but his §9 uses u_x ∈ {1, 2, 3}; the Gross–Zagier constant needs #μ(K)/2 (GrossZagierAndArithmeticHeights/E1).

sources.excerpt: u = [O×c : Z×] is half of the number of roots of unity in Oc
sources.match: u = #μ(K)/2 for c = 1; its square appears in the Gross–Zagier constant.

sources.excerpt: we will write ux to denote the cardinality of the group of roots of unity in K
sources.match: Read with the correction E1: u_x is half that cardinality, as on p. 119.

uses.how: The explicit Gross–Zagier constant has u² in the denominator.
Heegner points over K are normalised by 1/u.

nodes.title: The Artin-map convention and the Galois action on Heegner points
nodes.statement: The Gross–Zagier and Conrad convention sends uniformisers to arithmetic Frobenius elements. The opposite (geometric) convention is its composite with inversion on Gal(H/K). Under the arithmetic convention [a] ∈ Cl_K acts on the Heegner point ([b], n) by ([b][a]⁻¹, n). Every formula indexed by class-group characters χ changes χ to χ⁻¹ when the convention changes; a Gross–Zagier formula pairs χ with χ⁻¹ and is therefore stated together with its convention.
hypotheses: K imaginary quadratic with Hilbert class field H.
proofSteps: The two reciprocity maps Cl_K → Gal(H/K) differ by inversion, by definition.
The action on Heegner points is Conrad's statement, p. 69, which he derives from the analytic description C/b → C/n⁻¹b.
acceptance: A reciprocity law stated without its convention is not accepted.

sources.excerpt: we normalize the Artin map of class field theory to associate uniformizers to arithmetic Frobenius elements
sources.match: The Artin-map convention of Gross–Zagier, which Conrad follows.

sources.excerpt: The appearance of inversion is due to our decision to send uniformizers to arithmetic (rather than geometric) Frobenius elements
sources.match: Changing the Artin convention inverts the Galois action on Heegner points.

nodes.title: Full real period, identity-component period and c∞
nodes.statement: For E/ℚ with a minimal Weierstrass equation and Néron differential ω, let Ω⁰ be the least positive real period (∫ of |ω| over the identity component E(ℝ)⁰) and c∞ = #π₀(E(ℝ)), which is 2 if Δ > 0 and 1 if Δ < 0. The BSD real period is Ω = c∞·Ω⁰ = ∫_{E(ℝ)}|ω|, and it is what EllipticCurves Layer 7's integral 2∫_{D_W > 0} dx/√D_W computes. A formula stated with Ω⁰ must carry c∞ separately, and a formula stated with Ω must not multiply by c∞ again.
proofSteps: E(ℝ) has two components exactly when the cubic 4x³ + b₂x² + 2b₄x + b₆ has three real roots, i.e. Δ > 0.
The integral over E(ℝ) is the sum over its components, which have equal ∫|ω| because translation by a point of the non-identity component preserves |ω|.
acceptance: 37.a1 has Δ = 37 > 0, so c∞ = 2, and the LMFDB real period 5.9869172924… is the full period Ω = 2Ω⁰.

sources.excerpt: the least positive element of Λ∩ℝ multiplied by the number of components of E(ℝ)
sources.match: The BSD real period includes the factor c∞ = #π₀(E(ℝ)).

At f790474 the implemented canonicalHeight carries the factor 1/2 and regulator is the Gram determinant of the halved pairing, so it is 2^{−r}·Reg_BSD (37.a1: 0.02556 against LMFDB 0.05111). Layer 6's text pins ĥ = lim h(x(nP))/n², which is twice the implemented one. gaps.title: The [K:ℚ] normalisation of heights over number fields
gaps.detail: Tau Ceti's naïve height is Mathlib's logHeight for whatever Height.AdmissibleAbsValues instance is supplied, and neither library has an instance for number fields (Mathlib's Height/Basic.lean lists it as a TODO). Whether ĥ over K is the height over K (as in Cai–Shu–Tian's ĥ_K) or the absolute height (the LMFDB's base-change-invariant ĥ/[K:ℚ]) is therefore not yet fixed; the factor is [K:ℚ], and [K:ℚ]^r on regulators.

gaps.title: The Poincaré-biextension pairing against ⟨,⟩_BSD
gaps.detail: Cai–Shu–Tian's pairing A(K̄)_ℚ ⊗ A∨(K̄)_ℚ → ℝ, restricted to an elliptic curve through the principal polarisation P ↦ [P] − [O], should be ⟨,⟩_BSD (with the height over K). That comparison needs GZ.1's Poincaré construction, which this checkpoint does not plan.

sourceIssues.locator: §1, 'Some conventions', p. 69 (SLMath PDF p. 4); against §9, p. 119 (PDF p. 54)
sourceIssues.printed: If x is a Heegner point with associated CM field K, we will write ux to denote the cardinality of the group of roots of unity in K (so ux = 2 unless K = Q(√−1) or K = Q(√−3)).
sourceIssues.correction: u_x is half that cardinality (u_x = 1 unless K = Q(√−1), Q(√−3), where it is 2, 3), as p. 119 uses it and as in Gross–Zagier's u = #O_K^×/2.
sourceIssues.reason: On p. 119 the same symbol appears in 'The group AutF(x) … has order 2ux with ux ∈ {1, 2, 3}'. Aut_F(x) is the unit group of the CM order, of order #μ(K) ∈ {2, 4, 6}, so there u_x = #μ(K)/2. The two uses differ by a factor of 2, which becomes 4 in any formula with u_x².
